## Results

Synthesis and characterization of Ag/WO3
Unmodified WO3 was synthesized via a solvothermal method, utilizing WCl6 as the precursor. Subsequently, Ag/WO3 was synthesized via in situ reduction of Ag+ by low-valence W5+24. The detailed synthetic procedures can be found in the Methods section. As shown in Fig. 2a, the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of obtained samples exclusively exhibit peaks corresponding to monoclinic WO3 (JCPDS#83-0950). After the introduction of Ag, neither the peak positions nor the intensities in the XRD patterns show significant changes. To further analyze the W–O configuration, Raman spectroscopy was performed (Fig. 2b). The peak at 944 cm−1 corresponds to the W=O stretching vibration, while bands at 718 cm−1 and 794 cm−1 are characteristic of O–W–O stretching modes. Additionally, the signals at 261 cm−1 and 321 cm−1 represent the W–O–W stretching vibration25,26. The synthesized samples were further characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and N2 adsorption-desorption analysis. SEM images indicated that Ag/WO3 exhibits a spherical morphology with diameters ranging from 500 to 1000 nm (Supplementary Fig. 1). TEM-energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping confirmed the uniform distribution of Ag on the surface (Supplementary Fig. 2). Moreover, the presence of W and O was verified by XPS analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3). In comparison with pure WO3, the Ag/WO3 showed a slight decrease in specific surface area, which can be attributed to the repeated calcination process (Supplementary Fig. 4).

We further employed XPS to detect Ag elements in the sample. As illustrated in Fig. 2c, the high-resolution Ag 3d XPS spectrum of Ag/WO3 confirms the presence of the Ag element on the surface of Ag/WO3. The amount of Ag element is 1.68 wt%, as determined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (Supplementary Table 1). To look into the local coordination structure of Ag element in Ag/WO3, the X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectra were collected. In the Ag K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectrum (Fig. 2d), the white-line of the Ag K-edge for the Ag/WO3 catalyst is higher than that of the Ag foil and is close to that of Ag2O. This observation suggests that Ag element carries a fraction of positive charge, suggesting that there is charge transfer between Ag sites and carrier material27,28. Through density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we can clearly see that there is a charge transfer phenomenon between Ag and the support WO3 (Supplementary Fig. 5). The Fourier-transformed k3-weighted extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra show the main peak at 1.51 Å (Fig. 2e), corresponding to the first coordination shell of isolated Ag atoms27. The Ag−Ag peak at 2.65 Å is significantly weaker than the first-shell peak, confirming that Ag in the catalyst exist predominantly as dispersed single atoms. The wavelet transform (WT) plot of Ag/WO3 exhibited an intensity maximum at ~1.5 Å, corresponding to the Ag−O coordination (Supplementary Fig. 6), and pattern distinctly contrasts with the maxima observed in Ag foil (metallic Ag−Ag bonds), further confirmed the atomic dispersion state of Ag species in the Ag/WO3 system. Quantitative least-squares EXAFS analysis was further employed to investigate the coordination environment of single Ag atoms in Ag/WO3 (Fig. 2f). The fitting results indicate a first coordination shell with a coordination number of 3.86 for Ag−O and a second shell with 4.06 for Ag−W (Supplementary Table 2; Supplementary Fig. 7).

The light absorption properties of the synthesized catalysts were investigated using UV-Visible diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (UV-Vis DRS). Both WO3 and Ag/WO3 catalysts exhibit primary excitation by light with wavelengths below 500 nm (Supplementary Fig. 8). Interestingly, upon simulated sunlight irradiation, Ag/WO3 displays an increased absorption band within the 450–800 nm range (Fig. 2g). This phenomenon is attributed to the ability of visible or near-infrared light to induce polaron transitions, specifically the hopping of polarons from W5+ to adjacent W6+ positions23,26. During the initial 3 min of light irradiation, the peak intensity in the 450–800 nm range significantly increases, indicating an increased W5+ content in Ag/WO3. To further confirm that W5+ is involved in this process, in situ XPS analysis was performed on Ag/WO3 catalysts. The deconvolution of the W 4f XPS spectra revealed two valence states under both conditions, consisting of W5+ (with characteristic doublet at 35.9 eV for 4f 7/2 and 38.0 eV for 4f 5/2) and W6+ (with characteristic doublet at 34.5 eV for 4f 7/2 and 36.6 eV for 4f 5/2)29,30. Three-minute irradiation increased the W5+ proportion from 14.45% to 16.98% (Fig. 2h; Supplementary Fig. 9 and Supplementary Table 3). The switching of tungsten valence states between W6+ and W5+ indicates that the Ag/WO3 sample stores electrons in the catalyst during irradiation.

To investigate whether the stored electrons in Ag/WO3 can spontaneously release for reduction reaction, we employed 2,2,6,6-Tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) as a trapping agent to capture the stored electrons in the catalyst. TEMPO contains unpaired electrons, and typical three peaks can be observed via electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy31. Initially, we stirred TEMPO in the dark for 40 min, and no significant change in the EPR peak intensity was observed (Supplementary Fig. 10a), indicating that subsequent EPR signal variations are related to the added species. Subsequently, we introduced the newly prepared Ag/WO3 into the TEMPO solution. Upon initial addition, a slight decrease in the unpaired electron signal in the EPR was observed (Supplementary Fig. 10b). However, after continuing to stir, there was no further decrease in the EPR signal, suggesting that no electrons were released during the stirring process. Interestingly, when Ag/WO3 was irradiated with simulated sunlight for 10 min and then added to the TEMPO solution, the unpaired electron signal intensity in the EPR spectra continued to decrease during stirring, reaching a stable state after 30 min (Fig. 2i). This sustained decrease indicates that photo-generated electrons stored in Ag/WO3 can be released for reduction process.

Sustainable CO2 conversion performance of catalysts containing Ag/WO3 composites
To determine whether the electrons stored in the Ag/WO3 nanoparticles can effectively recombine with the photogenerated holes produced by the active components, we constructed a model catalyst, CoPc/Ag/WO3, by combining Ag/WO3 with the widely studied CoPc. The fundamental physicochemical properties of the CoPc/Ag/WO3 composite catalyst were characterized using XRD, XPS, SEM, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, and UV-Vis DRS (Supplementary Figs. 11–15). All these characterization results confirm that the synthesized composite material CoPc/Ag/WO3 is composed of Ag/WO3 and CoPc, which is consistent with the expected structure.

The CO2 reduction coupling with H2O oxidation performance of synthesized samples was evaluated under simulated solar irradiation by using a Xenon lamp source with an AM 1.5G filter. As shown in Fig. 3a, CoPc and Ag/WO3 exhibit minimal CO production during photocatalytic CO2 reduction, consistent with literature reports32,33. Under simulated solar irradiation, the CO production efficiency of the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst with the optimal ratio (10 wt%) reaches 0.148 mmol g−1 h−1. This observation implies that the combination of Ag/WO3 and CoPc can fulfill the requirements for CO2 reduction with H2O. When the content of CoPc in the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst is less than 10 wt%, there is an approximate linear relationship between the content of CoPc in the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst and the CO yield, showing a rate of ~1.5 mmol CO produced per gram of CoPc per hour (Supplementary Fig. 16). The efficiency of this catalyst is considered high compared to previous reports using CoPc in pure H2O systems, and it approaches the efficiency catalytic system using organic sacrificial agents (Fig. 3d; Supplementary Table 4). Additionally, we explored the catalytic performance of the composite catalyst (CoPc/WO3) composed of CoPc and WO3, which demonstrates a CO production rate of 0.017 mmol g−1 h−1. The CO generation rate of the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst is eight times higher than that of the CoPc/WO3 catalyst, indicating that Ag at the interface also plays an important role. By systematically varying the Ag content in CoPc/Ag/WO3, we observed that Ag has a significant impact on the catalytic efficiency of CO2 conversion (Supplementary Fig. 17), further confirming this point and highlighting the crucial role of the Ag in enhancing the CO2 reduction performance.

In addition to detecting CO, we also observed trace quantities of methane (CH4) for CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 18). CO remains the predominant product, exhibiting a carbon selectivity exceeding 90%. Through DFT calculations, we discovered that CoPc selectively produces CO rather than CH4, because converting CO to CH4 requires overcoming an energy barrier that is 0.65 eV higher than that for producing CO (Supplementary Fig. 19). This energy difference explains why CO becomes the dominant product. Additionally, we did not detect H2 in the products, which may be attributed to limited H2O-catalyst surface mass transfer process during the gas-solid phase process28. Moreover, we examined O2 evolution during H2O oxidation by CoPc/Ag/WO3, with the O2:CO molar ratio approaching 1:2, indicative of the synergistic coupling between CO2 reduction and H2O oxidation (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Fig. 20)7,34. To ascertain whether the production of CO stems from CO2 reduction, we conducted performance tests on the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst under high-purity Ar conditions. The results revealed only trace amount of CO, which could potentially originate from carbon impurities present within the catalyst35. To further explore this process, we replaced 12CO2 with 13CO2 and attempted to detect 13CO in the products. Following gas chromatography (GC) separation, mass spectrometry (MS) confirmed the existence of ion fragments (m/z = 13, 16, and 29) corresponding to 13CO (Fig. 3c). Based on the aforementioned evidence, we conclusively attribute the production of CO to CO2 reduction.

In practical applications, stability is of paramount importance of catalyst. Consequently, we subjected the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst to cyclic testing under simulated sunlight, over six cycles spanning 72 h of CO2 reduction reaction, the catalyst exhibited no significant deactivation (Supplementary Fig. 21). In addition, characterizations of the used CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst using XRD, FTIR, XAFS and XPS revealed no observable changes compared to the fresh one (Supplementary Figs. 22–25), affirming the excellent stability of the catalyst.

Effects of charge reservoir in Ag/WO3 for CoPc catalysts
Base on the characterization of Ag/WO3 and the evaluation of CO2 reduction performance in its composite catalysts, we have demonstrated that Ag/WO3 enables the storage and release of photogenerated electrons, and significantly enhances the CO2 reduction activity of the active component. This prompts us to investigate whether a potential link exists between the electron storage/release properties in Ag/WO3 and its improved CO2 reduction performance. Therefore, we selected the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst for further study to elucidate the mechanism of performance improvement.

We first determined the valence band (VB) position of Ag/WO3 using XPS VB spectra36. The obtained VB value of Ag/WO3 is ~2.93 V (Supplementary Fig. 26). Similarly, we determined the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of CoPc to be 0.90 V. Further analysis using the Kubelka–Munk function revealed that the band gaps of CoPc and Ag/WO3 are 1.89 eV and 2.75 eV, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 27). Based on the above information, we have obtained the band structure of CoPc and Ag/WO3, as shown in Fig. 4a. From the band structure, it can be seen that the charge transfer along the Z-scheme structure between CoPc and Ag/WO3 is the most conducive to achieving efficient CO2 reduction and H2O oxidation7,11,13. The formation of Z-scheme heterojunctions can be verified through the redox capabilities of generated electrons and holes. Photogenerated electrons can reduce O2 to ·O2− radicals (−0.33 V), while holes can oxidize H2O or OH− to ·OH radicals (2.39 V)12. Therefore, EPR spectroscopy was used to detect ·O2− and ·OH radicals using DMPO (5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide) as the spin-trapping agent. Under light irradiation, the characteristic peaks of DMPO-·O2− and DMPO-·OH in the CoPc/Ag/WO3 system appeared (Fig. 4b, c). For the CoPc catalyst, only the DMPO-·O2− peak appears; while in the Ag/WO3 system, only the DMPO-·OH peak is observed. In the CoPc/Ag/WO3 system do both DMPO-·O2− and DMPO-·OH peaks occur simultaneously, and their intensities are significantly higher than those of individual components. This suggests that in the CoPc/Ag/WO3 photocatalytic system, the electron-hole transfer pathway follows the Z-scheme, with the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of CoPc accumulates strongly reducing electrons, while VB of Ag/WO3 accumulates strongly oxidizing holes, resulting in increased production of ·O2− and ·OH radicals, consistent with our expectations.

To gain sight into the photoinduced electron transfer between Ag/WO3 and CoPc components, we employed femtosecond time-resolved transient absorption (fs-TA) spectroscopy. As shown in Fig. 4d, g, the positive signals observed in the 425–525 nm range are attributed to the excited-state absorption (ESA) of the CoPc component37, which originates from π electrons transitioning in the phthalocyanine (Pc) ring from the S0 state to the S1 state (S0 → S1). Meanwhile, the positive peak appearing in the 525–545 nm range corresponds to the ESA associated with the WO3 component (Supplementary Fig. 28). The negative ground-state bleaching (GSB) peaks in the 550–650 nm range arise from electron transfer from the Pc ligand to the Co sites (Pc → Co)37. In the fs-TA spectra of simulated sunlight irradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 (Fig. 4e, h), the ESA peak at 489 nm significantly enhanced compared to those of unirradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 (Fig. 4d, g). This increase in the number of electrons in the excited state of CoPc indicates that the recombination of electrons and holes within the phthalocyanine ring is effectively suppressed. The ESA signal in the 525–545 nm range, attributed to WO3 component, is also enhanced, implying an increased number of electrons in the excited state of WO3 and supporting the hypothesis that photogenerated electrons are stored in WO3. Additionally, the GSB peak of irradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 in the range of 550–650 nm range is also significantly enhanced (Fig. 4d, g). The stronger GSB peaks in irradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst compared to fresh CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst suggests a greater amount of photoinduced electron transfer from Pc to Co atom. These results demonstrate that the Ag/WO3 charge reservoir effectively scavenges photogenerated holes from CoPc, thereby maintaining a high electron density at the Co centers. This conclusion is further confirmed by time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) measurements, which show a reduced photoluminescence lifetime (Supplementary Fig. 29 and Supplementary Table 5).

To elucidate the role of the interfacial Ag, we also characterized the irradiated CoPc/WO3 catalyst using fs-TA spectroscopy, as shown in Fig. 4f, i. The ESA signal of the CoPc component was reduced, even though the ESA signal of the WO3 component remained largely unchanged. This result suggests that the electrons stored in WO3 cannot effectively extract or scavenge the photogenerated holes in the CoPc component, thereby leading to a decrease in the excited-state electron density of CoPc. Correspondingly, the GSB signal of the CoPc component in the range of 550–650 nm was significantly weaker in the pre-irradiated CoPc/WO3 sample than in the pre-irradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 sample, indicating suppressed electron transfer from the Pc ring to the Co atom. It is possible that the charge excited on Pc is primarily recombined rather than being transferred to the active sites, suggesting that single Ag atoms can serve as electron bridges, facilitating electron transfer across the interface. This interpretation is further corroborated by the smaller reduction in the average fluorescence lifetime in the Ag-free sample compared to the Ag-containing counterpart (Supplementary Fig. 30 and Supplementary Table 5). In addition, photocurrent and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy measurements are consistent with this conclusion (Supplementary Figs. 31–32). To further explore the role of Ag, we conducted in situ FTIR spectroscopy study on the CO2 conversion process over CoPc/Ag/WO3 and CoPc/WO3. The results showed that the introduction of Ag did not create new active sites for CO2 (Supplementary Fig. 33). This indicates that the main role of the interfacial Ag single atoms is to kinetically enhance the electron transfer at the interface.

The light-assisted Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy (KPFM) was employed to study the separation and transport behavior of photo-induced charge carriers of the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst before and after irradiation. The surface photovoltage (SPV) distribution of CoPc/Ag/WO3 is consistent with the height profile displayed by atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Supplementary Fig. 34), indicating that the changes in photovoltage before and after irradiation are related to the catalysts. After light irradiation, the SPV signal of CoPc/Ag/WO3 decreased by approximately −50 mV, while the catalyst was irradiated by simulated sunlight for 10 min decreased significantly by −100 mV. According to previous reports, a more negative SPV signal change represents a higher concentration of photogenerated electrons after light irradiation17,38. The negative SPV response of preirradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 is ~50 mV greater than that of fresh CoPc/Ag/WO3, indicating that photo-charged catalyst accelerates the concentrated accumulation of photogenerated electrons on the catalyst surface.

The universality of the charge reservoir strategy
Following the discovery that stored photogenerated electrons enhance the catalytic activity, assessing the universality of this charge storage mechanism becomes crucial. Therefore, we employed XPS VB spectra to investigate the distribution of accumulated electrons39. Through the XPS VB spectrum test, we found that after the sites of W5+ were introduced into the catalyst, a new peak appeared in the range of 0.3–1.5 V (centered at 0.9 V) (Fig. 5a, b). This means that as long as the oxidation potential of the photogenerated holes produced by the active components is greater than 0.3 V, accumulated electrons can be consumed, which greatly broadens the selection of active components.

To explore the potential application of Ag/WO3 in diverse catalytic systems, we prepared composite catalysts by combining it with two representative catalyst types: the polymer catalyst C3N4 (yielding C3N4/Ag/WO3) and the metal oxide Cu2O (yielding Cu2O/Ag/WO3). The CO2 reduction performance of these composites was evaluated under simulated sunlight. The C3N4/Ag/WO3 composite exhibited substantially enhanced CO2 reduction activity compared to unmodified C3N4. At the optimal C3N4 loading of 50 wt%, the CO and CH4 production rates reached 0.123 and 0.064 mmol g−1 h−1, respectively (Fig. 5c). This represents a 5.5-fold increase in CO yield and a 23.8-fold increase in CH4 yield over the pure C3N4, which produced CO and CH4 at only 0.022 and 0.003 mmol g−1 h−1, respectively. The pronounced enhancement in CH4 production, which involves an 8-electron transfer process compared to the 2-electron pathway for CO, suggests a significant improvement in the electron supply capability of the active sites. Similarly, the optimal composite with 40 wt% Cu2O loading achieved a CO production rate of 0.070 mmol g−1 h−1 (Fig. 5d), which is 11.7 times higher than that of the pure Cu2O catalyst (0.006 mmol g−1 h−1). These results collectively confirm that the Ag/WO3 can be used in diverse catalyst systems, highlighting the potential for further applications in high-value product synthesis.

To investigate whether Ag/WO3 remains effective under natural sunlight, we conducted an outdoor CO2 reduction test on CoPc/Ag/WO3 using natural sunlight. A demonstration experimental device was constructed, incorporating a Fresnel lens to concentrate sunlight onto the catalyst surface (Supplementary Fig. 35). Solar irradiance was recorded at one-minute intervals throughout the test, as illustrated in Fig. 5e. Gas samples (2 mL each) were collected on the hour from 6:00 to 20:00 for analysis (Fig. 5g, h). Before solar irradiation reached the catalyst (6:00–7:00), no products were detected. Although sunlight began to illuminate the catalyst around 7:25, the CO signal remained negligible at 8:00 due to low light intensity. Measurable CO production was not observed until 9:00. The hourly CO yield reached a maximum of 9.3 μmol between 13:00 and 14:00. After 17:50, solar irradiation was no longer sufficient to maintain the reaction. Accordingly, no further increase in CO concentration was observed after the 18:00 sampling point. The variation in CO generation rate closely followed the trend of solar light intensity (Fig. 5e, g), confirming that natural sunlight can effectively trigger the CO2-to-CO reduction reaction. Although there is still plenty of room to improve overall efficiency, likely due to limitations in light collection by the simple reaction setup, our results suggest the synthesized catalyst can be trigger by nature light.

## Methods

Synthesis of the WO3 catalyst
1 g of tungsten hexachloride (WCl6) was dissolved in 60 mL of ethanol. The solution was continuously stirred at room temperature for 30 min. Subsequently, the solution was transferred to a Teflon-lined autoclave, where it underwent treatment at 180 °C for 12 h. Following this process, the suspension was subjected to centrifugation, followed by repeated washes with ethanol and deionized H2O. Finally, the obtained material was dried at 70 °C and subsequently calcined in an air atmosphere at 300 °C for 1 h, resulting in the formation of the desired WO3 catalyst.

Synthesis of Ag/WO3 catalyst
100 mg of WO3 was added to 50 mL of deionized H2O, followed by ultrasonic dispersion for 1 h to achieve a homogeneous dispersion solution; the mixture was purged with Ar for 1 h and irradiated using a 300 W xenon lamp for 1 h, during which the color changed to light blue, indicating the formation of reduced W5+. Subsequently, 3 mL of silver nitrate solution (AgNO3, 1 mg/mL) was introduced into the dispersed solution and stirred at room temperature for 1 min; after stirring, the solid catalyst was separated via centrifugation and alternately washed three times with absolute ethanol and deionized H2O. Finally, the washed catalyst was dried at 70 °C in air and calcined in an air atmosphere at 300 °C for 1 h, yielding a light-yellow product corresponding to Ag/WO3; the procedure was replicated to prepare samples with varying Ag contents by adjusting the AgNO3 addition amount accordingly.

Synthesis of composite catalyst
10 mg of cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc, analytical grade) was dissolved in 50 mL of absolute ethanol, followed by 3 h of ultrasonic treatment at room temperature. Subsequently, 90 mg of Ag/WO3 was added to the mixture, and an additional hour of ultrasonic treatment was applied. The dispersion was then ball-milled at 500 rpm for 5 h. Next, the ultrasonically treated catalyst was stirred at 85 °C until all the ethanol had evaporated. The resulting dried catalyst was washed three times with absolute ethanol and air-dried at 70 °C. The resulting catalyst is denoted as CoPc/Ag/WO3. The synthesis steps for other proportional CoPc catalysts remain the same as described above, with the only variation being the ratio of CoPc added. By substituting Ag/WO3 with WO3, while keeping the other steps unchanged, the resulting catalyst is CoPc/WO3. The detailed synthesis procedures for Cu2O and highly crystalline C3N4 are described in the Supporting Information. Upon obtaining the individual Cu2O and C3N4 monomers, the Cu2O/Ag/WO3 catalyst and the C3N4/Ag/WO3 composite catalyst were respectively prepared following a synthesis procedure analogous to that used for CoPc/Ag/WO3.

General characterization
The XRD patterns were tested using a Panalytical X’pert Pro X-ray diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.5406 Å, 40 kV, 40 mA). Raman spectra were recorded using a Raman microscope imaging spectrometer (Thermo Scientific DXR2xi, USA). XPS data were recorded using a Thermo ESCALAB 250 X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (USA). All the binding energies were referenced to the C 1s peak at 284.8 eV. To present the data intuitively, the data presented in the VB spectrum have been calibrated using the contact potential difference and the work function of the instrument36,40. EPR spectra were collected by a ELEXSYS E500 spectrometer (Bruker, Germany) at room temperature. Ag K-edge XAFS spectrum was collected at the 14W1 beamline in Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility. UV-Vis DRS spectra were carried on a Varian Cary 100 Scan UV-Vis system with BaSO4 as the reflectance standard. The transient absorption setup utilized an Yb:KGW laser in conjunction with the pump-probe transient absorption spectrometer (TA100, Time-Tech Spectra, LLC). The fundamental beam was split into two branches. One branch was directed into an optical parametric amplifier to generate the pump pulse. Meanwhile, the broadband probe pulse (ranging from 300 to 1000 nm) was produced by focusing the fundamental pulse onto a sapphire crystal. At the sample position, the focal size of pump was adjusted to be significantly larger than that of the probe, ensuring nearly homogeneous excitation density in the probed area. The samples were pumped at 360 nm and coated onto quartz glass for testing.

Evaluation of CO2 conversion performance
The photocatalytic activity of the as-prepared samples for CO2 reduction was investigated using a custom-made cylindrical stainless-steel reactor (volume = 200 mL) equipped with a quartz window. The photocatalysts (5 mg) were uniformly dispersed in 3 mL of deionized H2O and then transferred to a dish (50 mm in diameter). The dish was subsequently dried under vacuum at 70 °C for 24 h to coat it with the sample. Next, the dish with the sample was placed inside the reactor, and 1 mL of deionized H2O was added to the reactor. The reactor was purged with high-purity CO2 three times. Following this, a specific amount of high-purity CO2 was introduced into the reactor to maintain a pressure of 1 bar. Simulated sunlight was generated using a 300 W Xe arc lamp with an AM 1.5G filter, which irradiated the sample through the quartz window. The resulting products were analyzed using gas chromatography (7890B, Agilent). The instrument was equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) to detect CH4 and CO, as well as a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) to detect O2 and H2. In the isotope labeling experiment, we substituted 13CO2 for 12CO2 as the reactant, and the resulting product was detected using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (7890A and 5975C, Agilent).

In our study, O2 was quantitatively analyzed using gas chromatography with a thermal conductivity detector (GC-TCD). To ensure measurement accuracy and address potential air leakage concerns, we implemented the following approaches throughout the photocatalytic reaction. First, all gas sampling was performed using an automated online system to prevent leakage during the sampling process. Second, we continuously monitored N2 levels as an indicator of potential air intrusion. Prior to the reaction, the reactor was rigorously purged with high-purity CO2 (>99.999%) through multiple evacuation-refill cycles. Under our GC-TCD configuration, O2 and N2 exhibit well-resolved peaks at approximately 4.4 min and 5.9 min, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 20a). To further ensure accuracy, the detected O2 concentration was corrected by subtracting the contribution from any residual air based on the measured N2 signal, using the following equation:
n_reaction_O2 = n_O2 - n_N2 * (20.9% / 78.1%)
where n_reaction_O2 is the final amount of O2 produced from the reaction, n_O2 is the amount of O2 measured by GC-TCD, and n_N2 is the amount of N2 measured by GC-TCD. The factors 20.9% and 78.1% represent the volume fractions of O2 and N2 in air, respectively.
This correction, along with the consistent N2 level and clear O2 evolution trend, strongly supports the stoichiometric coupling observed between O2 and CO production (O2:CO ≈ 1:2). We have included a detailed description of the methodology and validation data in the revised Supporting Information.

## Paper

## Abstract

Solar-driven conversion of CO2 and H2O into chemicals is a promising strategy, while achieving simultaneous and efficient CO2 reduction and H2O oxidation remains challenging. Here, inspired by the role of plastoquinone in temporarily storing electrons during natural photosynthesis, we design a silver-modified tungsten trioxide (Ag/WO3) that functions as a charge reservoir through reversible W6+/W5+ transitions under irradiation. When coupled with various active components, Ag/WO3 significantly enhances their CO2 conversion performance, indicating the universality of this strategy. Specifically, coupling Ag/WO3 with cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst achieves a CO production rate of ~1.5 mmol g−1 h−1, representing a 100-fold enhancement over pure CoPc. Mechanistic studies reveal that electrons stored in Ag/WO3 efficiently scavenge photogenerated holes from CoPc, thereby maintaining a high electron density at CO2 reduction sites of CoPc. This work establishes a bioinspired charge reservoir strategy for efficient CO2 photoreduction, providing a universal approach to solar fuel production.

---

## Introduction

Solar-driven photocatalytic reduction of CO2 into value-added chemicals has attracted considerable interest, as it offers a promising route to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions and alleviate resource constraints1–6. In recent decades, the use of organic sacrificial agents (e.g., triethanolamine or triethylamine) has significantly enhanced photocatalytic CO2 conversion performance, achieving rates ranging from tens to thousands of micromoles per gram per hour7,8. However, their irreversible consumption and potential interference with accurate performance evaluation hinder practical application9.

Water (H2O), being earth-abundant, represents an ideal hole scavenger. Nevertheless, its four-electron oxidation process, with an oxidation potential of +0.83 V (vs. NHE, pH = 7, hereafter the same), presents substantial thermodynamic and kinetic limitations, impeding efficient hole extraction and sustainable CO2 reduction10–12. To address these challenges, photocatalytic systems must overcome two inherent limitations in CO2 reduction with H2O: both half-reactions involve multiple electron transfers and require simultaneous accumulation of electrons and holes at distinct surface sites. Furthermore, the two half-reactions are tightly coupled and interdependent, necessitating not only matched migration rates of photogenerated electrons and holes to the surface but also kinetically balanced surface redox reactions7. Constructing a Z-scheme heterojunction, inspired by natural photosynthesis and integrating two narrow-bandgap semiconductors, has been regarded as an effective strategy to overcome these obstacles13,14. Exemplary systems include 3D-SiC@2D-MoS2 7, AgVO3/TiO2 15, MoS2/Fe2O3 16, among others. However, a key challenge still remains: the significant difference in electron and hole transport dynamics requires spatiotemporal coupled charge migration17, which results in the absence of a universal strategy for constructing composite structures applicable to the vast majority of active components.

Natural photosynthesis achieves remarkable efficiency in coupling CO2 reduction and H2O oxidation through sophisticated charge management: Photosystem II (PSII) and Photosystem I (PSI) are spatially and temporally separated and combine with reversible electron carriers for directional energy transfer18,19. In this system, PSII exclusively drives H2O oxidation (2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e⁻), while the liberated electrons are temporarily stored and buffered by quinone carriers like plastoquinone (PQ) through reversible redox reactions before being delivered to PSI for the synthesis of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH)20,21, which is essential for subsequent CO2 reduction (Fig. 1a). In this process, PQ enables the temporary storage of short-lived photogenerated electrons, ensuring efficient electron transfer between PSI and PSII. Inspired by this natural strategy, we considered introducing a similar charge storage strategy into an artificial photosynthetic system through a redox medium, enabling the reaction of the composite material to decouple the functions of H2O oxidation and CO2 reduction in time, and developed a general interfacial charge transfer strategy.

Our previous studies demonstrated that the conversion of W6+ to W5+ in tungsten oxide (WO3) allows for the transient trapping and storage of photogenerated electrons22,23. If these stored photogenerated electrons can be extracted to recombine with photogenerated holes in the CO2 reduction active components, they would function analogously to PQ. To validate this, we synthesized a silver single-atom-anchored WO3 material (Ag/WO3) and demonstrated that Ag/WO3 can effectively store photoexcited electrons through irradiation-induced W6+/W5+ valence oscillation (Fig. 1b). As verification experiments, subsequent separate coupling of Ag/WO3 with extensively studied active components, including cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), graphitic carbon nitride (C3N4), and cuprous oxide (Cu2O), yields composite catalysts exhibiting substantially enhanced performance relative to the pristine catalysts. Detailed characterization of the most effective model catalyst, CoPc/Ag/WO3, reveals that stored photoexcited electrons in Ag/WO3 migrate to recombine with photogenerated holes in CoPc. This process maintains a high density of reducing electrons at the CO2 reduction sites of CoPc. The CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst achieves a 100-fold enhancement in photocatalytic CO2 reduction activity compared to pure CoPc, matching the performance of optimized CoPc systems employing organic sacrificial agents. This bioinspired charge reservoir strategy demonstrates universal applicability across different catalytic systems, providing a sustainable and universal strategy for photocatalyst development in CO2 conversion.

---

## Results

Synthesis and characterization of Ag/WO3
Unmodified WO3 was synthesized via a solvothermal method, utilizing WCl6 as the precursor. Subsequently, Ag/WO3 was synthesized via in situ reduction of Ag+ by low-valence W5+24. The detailed synthetic procedures can be found in the Methods section. As shown in Fig. 2a, the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of obtained samples exclusively exhibit peaks corresponding to monoclinic WO3 (JCPDS#83-0950). After the introduction of Ag, neither the peak positions nor the intensities in the XRD patterns show significant changes. To further analyze the W–O configuration, Raman spectroscopy was performed (Fig. 2b). The peak at 944 cm−1 corresponds to the W=O stretching vibration, while bands at 718 cm−1 and 794 cm−1 are characteristic of O–W–O stretching modes. Additionally, the signals at 261 cm−1 and 321 cm−1 represent the W–O–W stretching vibration25,26. The synthesized samples were further characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and N2 adsorption-desorption analysis. SEM images indicated that Ag/WO3 exhibits a spherical morphology with diameters ranging from 500 to 1000 nm (Supplementary Fig. 1). TEM-energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping confirmed the uniform distribution of Ag on the surface (Supplementary Fig. 2). Moreover, the presence of W and O was verified by XPS analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3). In comparison with pure WO3, the Ag/WO3 showed a slight decrease in specific surface area, which can be attributed to the repeated calcination process (Supplementary Fig. 4).

We further employed XPS to detect Ag elements in the sample. As illustrated in Fig. 2c, the high-resolution Ag 3d XPS spectrum of Ag/WO3 confirms the presence of the Ag element on the surface of Ag/WO3. The amount of Ag element is 1.68 wt%, as determined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (Supplementary Table 1). To look into the local coordination structure of Ag element in Ag/WO3, the X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectra were collected. In the Ag K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectrum (Fig. 2d), the white-line of the Ag K-edge for the Ag/WO3 catalyst is higher than that of the Ag foil and is close to that of Ag2O. This observation suggests that Ag element carries a fraction of positive charge, suggesting that there is charge transfer between Ag sites and carrier material27,28. Through density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we can clearly see that there is a charge transfer phenomenon between Ag and the support WO3 (Supplementary Fig. 5). The Fourier-transformed k3-weighted extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra show the main peak at 1.51 Å (Fig. 2e), corresponding to the first coordination shell of isolated Ag atoms27. The Ag−Ag peak at 2.65 Å is significantly weaker than the first-shell peak, confirming that Ag in the catalyst exist predominantly as dispersed single atoms. The wavelet transform (WT) plot of Ag/WO3 exhibited an intensity maximum at ~1.5 Å, corresponding to the Ag−O coordination (Supplementary Fig. 6), and pattern distinctly contrasts with the maxima observed in Ag foil (metallic Ag−Ag bonds), further confirmed the atomic dispersion state of Ag species in the Ag/WO3 system. Quantitative least-squares EXAFS analysis was further employed to investigate the coordination environment of single Ag atoms in Ag/WO3 (Fig. 2f). The fitting results indicate a first coordination shell with a coordination number of 3.86 for Ag−O and a second shell with 4.06 for Ag−W (Supplementary Table 2; Supplementary Fig. 7).

The light absorption properties of the synthesized catalysts were investigated using UV-Visible diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (UV-Vis DRS). Both WO3 and Ag/WO3 catalysts exhibit primary excitation by light with wavelengths below 500 nm (Supplementary Fig. 8). Interestingly, upon simulated sunlight irradiation, Ag/WO3 displays an increased absorption band within the 450–800 nm range (Fig. 2g). This phenomenon is attributed to the ability of visible or near-infrared light to induce polaron transitions, specifically the hopping of polarons from W5+ to adjacent W6+ positions23,26. During the initial 3 min of light irradiation, the peak intensity in the 450–800 nm range significantly increases, indicating an increased W5+ content in Ag/WO3. To further confirm that W5+ is involved in this process, in situ XPS analysis was performed on Ag/WO3 catalysts. The deconvolution of the W 4f XPS spectra revealed two valence states under both conditions, consisting of W5+ (with characteristic doublet at 35.9 eV for 4f 7/2 and 38.0 eV for 4f 5/2) and W6+ (with characteristic doublet at 34.5 eV for 4f 7/2 and 36.6 eV for 4f 5/2)29,30. Three-minute irradiation increased the W5+ proportion from 14.45% to 16.98% (Fig. 2h; Supplementary Fig. 9 and Supplementary Table 3). The switching of tungsten valence states between W6+ and W5+ indicates that the Ag/WO3 sample stores electrons in the catalyst during irradiation.

To investigate whether the stored electrons in Ag/WO3 can spontaneously release for reduction reaction, we employed 2,2,6,6-Tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) as a trapping agent to capture the stored electrons in the catalyst. TEMPO contains unpaired electrons, and typical three peaks can be observed via electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy31. Initially, we stirred TEMPO in the dark for 40 min, and no significant change in the EPR peak intensity was observed (Supplementary Fig. 10a), indicating that subsequent EPR signal variations are related to the added species. Subsequently, we introduced the newly prepared Ag/WO3 into the TEMPO solution. Upon initial addition, a slight decrease in the unpaired electron signal in the EPR was observed (Supplementary Fig. 10b). However, after continuing to stir, there was no further decrease in the EPR signal, suggesting that no electrons were released during the stirring process. Interestingly, when Ag/WO3 was irradiated with simulated sunlight for 10 min and then added to the TEMPO solution, the unpaired electron signal intensity in the EPR spectra continued to decrease during stirring, reaching a stable state after 30 min (Fig. 2i). This sustained decrease indicates that photo-generated electrons stored in Ag/WO3 can be released for reduction process.

Sustainable CO2 conversion performance of catalysts containing Ag/WO3 composites
To determine whether the electrons stored in the Ag/WO3 nanoparticles can effectively recombine with the photogenerated holes produced by the active components, we constructed a model catalyst, CoPc/Ag/WO3, by combining Ag/WO3 with the widely studied CoPc. The fundamental physicochemical properties of the CoPc/Ag/WO3 composite catalyst were characterized using XRD, XPS, SEM, Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, and UV-Vis DRS (Supplementary Figs. 11–15). All these characterization results confirm that the synthesized composite material CoPc/Ag/WO3 is composed of Ag/WO3 and CoPc, which is consistent with the expected structure.

The CO2 reduction coupling with H2O oxidation performance of synthesized samples was evaluated under simulated solar irradiation by using a Xenon lamp source with an AM 1.5G filter. As shown in Fig. 3a, CoPc and Ag/WO3 exhibit minimal CO production during photocatalytic CO2 reduction, consistent with literature reports32,33. Under simulated solar irradiation, the CO production efficiency of the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst with the optimal ratio (10 wt%) reaches 0.148 mmol g−1 h−1. This observation implies that the combination of Ag/WO3 and CoPc can fulfill the requirements for CO2 reduction with H2O. When the content of CoPc in the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst is less than 10 wt%, there is an approximate linear relationship between the content of CoPc in the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst and the CO yield, showing a rate of ~1.5 mmol CO produced per gram of CoPc per hour (Supplementary Fig. 16). The efficiency of this catalyst is considered high compared to previous reports using CoPc in pure H2O systems, and it approaches the efficiency catalytic system using organic sacrificial agents (Fig. 3d; Supplementary Table 4). Additionally, we explored the catalytic performance of the composite catalyst (CoPc/WO3) composed of CoPc and WO3, which demonstrates a CO production rate of 0.017 mmol g−1 h−1. The CO generation rate of the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst is eight times higher than that of the CoPc/WO3 catalyst, indicating that Ag at the interface also plays an important role. By systematically varying the Ag content in CoPc/Ag/WO3, we observed that Ag has a significant impact on the catalytic efficiency of CO2 conversion (Supplementary Fig. 17), further confirming this point and highlighting the crucial role of the Ag in enhancing the CO2 reduction performance.

In addition to detecting CO, we also observed trace quantities of methane (CH4) for CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst (Supplementary Fig. 18). CO remains the predominant product, exhibiting a carbon selectivity exceeding 90%. Through DFT calculations, we discovered that CoPc selectively produces CO rather than CH4, because converting CO to CH4 requires overcoming an energy barrier that is 0.65 eV higher than that for producing CO (Supplementary Fig. 19). This energy difference explains why CO becomes the dominant product. Additionally, we did not detect H2 in the products, which may be attributed to limited H2O-catalyst surface mass transfer process during the gas-solid phase process28. Moreover, we examined O2 evolution during H2O oxidation by CoPc/Ag/WO3, with the O2:CO molar ratio approaching 1:2, indicative of the synergistic coupling between CO2 reduction and H2O oxidation (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Fig. 20)7,34. To ascertain whether the production of CO stems from CO2 reduction, we conducted performance tests on the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst under high-purity Ar conditions. The results revealed only trace amount of CO, which could potentially originate from carbon impurities present within the catalyst35. To further explore this process, we replaced 12CO2 with 13CO2 and attempted to detect 13CO in the products. Following gas chromatography (GC) separation, mass spectrometry (MS) confirmed the existence of ion fragments (m/z = 13, 16, and 29) corresponding to 13CO (Fig. 3c). Based on the aforementioned evidence, we conclusively attribute the production of CO to CO2 reduction.

In practical applications, stability is of paramount importance of catalyst. Consequently, we subjected the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst to cyclic testing under simulated sunlight, over six cycles spanning 72 h of CO2 reduction reaction, the catalyst exhibited no significant deactivation (Supplementary Fig. 21). In addition, characterizations of the used CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst using XRD, FTIR, XAFS and XPS revealed no observable changes compared to the fresh one (Supplementary Figs. 22–25), affirming the excellent stability of the catalyst.

Effects of charge reservoir in Ag/WO3 for CoPc catalysts
Base on the characterization of Ag/WO3 and the evaluation of CO2 reduction performance in its composite catalysts, we have demonstrated that Ag/WO3 enables the storage and release of photogenerated electrons, and significantly enhances the CO2 reduction activity of the active component. This prompts us to investigate whether a potential link exists between the electron storage/release properties in Ag/WO3 and its improved CO2 reduction performance. Therefore, we selected the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst for further study to elucidate the mechanism of performance improvement.

We first determined the valence band (VB) position of Ag/WO3 using XPS VB spectra36. The obtained VB value of Ag/WO3 is ~2.93 V (Supplementary Fig. 26). Similarly, we determined the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of CoPc to be 0.90 V. Further analysis using the Kubelka–Munk function revealed that the band gaps of CoPc and Ag/WO3 are 1.89 eV and 2.75 eV, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 27). Based on the above information, we have obtained the band structure of CoPc and Ag/WO3, as shown in Fig. 4a. From the band structure, it can be seen that the charge transfer along the Z-scheme structure between CoPc and Ag/WO3 is the most conducive to achieving efficient CO2 reduction and H2O oxidation7,11,13. The formation of Z-scheme heterojunctions can be verified through the redox capabilities of generated electrons and holes. Photogenerated electrons can reduce O2 to ·O2− radicals (−0.33 V), while holes can oxidize H2O or OH− to ·OH radicals (2.39 V)12. Therefore, EPR spectroscopy was used to detect ·O2− and ·OH radicals using DMPO (5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide) as the spin-trapping agent. Under light irradiation, the characteristic peaks of DMPO-·O2− and DMPO-·OH in the CoPc/Ag/WO3 system appeared (Fig. 4b, c). For the CoPc catalyst, only the DMPO-·O2− peak appears; while in the Ag/WO3 system, only the DMPO-·OH peak is observed. In the CoPc/Ag/WO3 system do both DMPO-·O2− and DMPO-·OH peaks occur simultaneously, and their intensities are significantly higher than those of individual components. This suggests that in the CoPc/Ag/WO3 photocatalytic system, the electron-hole transfer pathway follows the Z-scheme, with the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of CoPc accumulates strongly reducing electrons, while VB of Ag/WO3 accumulates strongly oxidizing holes, resulting in increased production of ·O2− and ·OH radicals, consistent with our expectations.

To gain sight into the photoinduced electron transfer between Ag/WO3 and CoPc components, we employed femtosecond time-resolved transient absorption (fs-TA) spectroscopy. As shown in Fig. 4d, g, the positive signals observed in the 425–525 nm range are attributed to the excited-state absorption (ESA) of the CoPc component37, which originates from π electrons transitioning in the phthalocyanine (Pc) ring from the S0 state to the S1 state (S0 → S1). Meanwhile, the positive peak appearing in the 525–545 nm range corresponds to the ESA associated with the WO3 component (Supplementary Fig. 28). The negative ground-state bleaching (GSB) peaks in the 550–650 nm range arise from electron transfer from the Pc ligand to the Co sites (Pc → Co)37. In the fs-TA spectra of simulated sunlight irradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 (Fig. 4e, h), the ESA peak at 489 nm significantly enhanced compared to those of unirradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 (Fig. 4d, g). This increase in the number of electrons in the excited state of CoPc indicates that the recombination of electrons and holes within the phthalocyanine ring is effectively suppressed. The ESA signal in the 525–545 nm range, attributed to WO3 component, is also enhanced, implying an increased number of electrons in the excited state of WO3 and supporting the hypothesis that photogenerated electrons are stored in WO3. Additionally, the GSB peak of irradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 in the range of 550–650 nm range is also significantly enhanced (Fig. 4d, g). The stronger GSB peaks in irradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst compared to fresh CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst suggests a greater amount of photoinduced electron transfer from Pc to Co atom. These results demonstrate that the Ag/WO3 charge reservoir effectively scavenges photogenerated holes from CoPc, thereby maintaining a high electron density at the Co centers. This conclusion is further confirmed by time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) measurements, which show a reduced photoluminescence lifetime (Supplementary Fig. 29 and Supplementary Table 5).

To elucidate the role of the interfacial Ag, we also characterized the irradiated CoPc/WO3 catalyst using fs-TA spectroscopy, as shown in Fig. 4f, i. The ESA signal of the CoPc component was reduced, even though the ESA signal of the WO3 component remained largely unchanged. This result suggests that the electrons stored in WO3 cannot effectively extract or scavenge the photogenerated holes in the CoPc component, thereby leading to a decrease in the excited-state electron density of CoPc. Correspondingly, the GSB signal of the CoPc component in the range of 550–650 nm was significantly weaker in the pre-irradiated CoPc/WO3 sample than in the pre-irradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 sample, indicating suppressed electron transfer from the Pc ring to the Co atom. It is possible that the charge excited on Pc is primarily recombined rather than being transferred to the active sites, suggesting that single Ag atoms can serve as electron bridges, facilitating electron transfer across the interface. This interpretation is further corroborated by the smaller reduction in the average fluorescence lifetime in the Ag-free sample compared to the Ag-containing counterpart (Supplementary Fig. 30 and Supplementary Table 5). In addition, photocurrent and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy measurements are consistent with this conclusion (Supplementary Figs. 31–32). To further explore the role of Ag, we conducted in situ FTIR spectroscopy study on the CO2 conversion process over CoPc/Ag/WO3 and CoPc/WO3. The results showed that the introduction of Ag did not create new active sites for CO2 (Supplementary Fig. 33). This indicates that the main role of the interfacial Ag single atoms is to kinetically enhance the electron transfer at the interface.

The light-assisted Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy (KPFM) was employed to study the separation and transport behavior of photo-induced charge carriers of the CoPc/Ag/WO3 catalyst before and after irradiation. The surface photovoltage (SPV) distribution of CoPc/Ag/WO3 is consistent with the height profile displayed by atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Supplementary Fig. 34), indicating that the changes in photovoltage before and after irradiation are related to the catalysts. After light irradiation, the SPV signal of CoPc/Ag/WO3 decreased by approximately −50 mV, while the catalyst was irradiated by simulated sunlight for 10 min decreased significantly by −100 mV. According to previous reports, a more negative SPV signal change represents a higher concentration of photogenerated electrons after light irradiation17,38. The negative SPV response of preirradiated CoPc/Ag/WO3 is ~50 mV greater than that of fresh CoPc/Ag/WO3, indicating that photo-charged catalyst accelerates the concentrated accumulation of photogenerated electrons on the catalyst surface.

The universality of the charge reservoir strategy
Following the discovery that stored photogenerated electrons enhance the catalytic activity, assessing the universality of this charge storage mechanism becomes crucial. Therefore, we employed XPS VB spectra to investigate the distribution of accumulated electrons39. Through the XPS VB spectrum test, we found that after the sites of W5+ were introduced into the catalyst, a new peak appeared in the range of 0.3–1.5 V (centered at 0.9 V) (Fig. 5a, b). This means that as long as the oxidation potential of the photogenerated holes produced by the active components is greater than 0.3 V, accumulated electrons can be consumed, which greatly broadens the selection of active components.

To explore the potential application of Ag/WO3 in diverse catalytic systems, we prepared composite catalysts by combining it with two representative catalyst types: the polymer catalyst C3N4 (yielding C3N4/Ag/WO3) and the metal oxide Cu2O (yielding Cu2O/Ag/WO3). The CO2 reduction performance of these composites was evaluated under simulated sunlight. The C3N4/Ag/WO3 composite exhibited substantially enhanced CO2 reduction activity compared to unmodified C3N4. At the optimal C3N4 loading of 50 wt%, the CO and CH4 production rates reached 0.123 and 0.064 mmol g−1 h−1, respectively (Fig. 5c). This represents a 5.5-fold increase in CO yield and a 23.8-fold increase in CH4 yield over the pure C3N4, which produced CO and CH4 at only 0.022 and 0.003 mmol g−1 h−1, respectively. The pronounced enhancement in CH4 production, which involves an 8-electron transfer process compared to the 2-electron pathway for CO, suggests a significant improvement in the electron supply capability of the active sites. Similarly, the optimal composite with 40 wt% Cu2O loading achieved a CO production rate of 0.070 mmol g−1 h−1 (Fig. 5d), which is 11.7 times higher than that of the pure Cu2O catalyst (0.006 mmol g−1 h−1). These results collectively confirm that the Ag/WO3 can be used in diverse catalyst systems, highlighting the potential for further applications in high-value product synthesis.

To investigate whether Ag/WO3 remains effective under natural sunlight, we conducted an outdoor CO2 reduction test on CoPc/Ag/WO3 using natural sunlight. A demonstration experimental device was constructed, incorporating a Fresnel lens to concentrate sunlight onto the catalyst surface (Supplementary Fig. 35). Solar irradiance was recorded at one-minute intervals throughout the test, as illustrated in Fig. 5e. Gas samples (2 mL each) were collected on the hour from 6:00 to 20:00 for analysis (Fig. 5g, h). Before solar irradiation reached the catalyst (6:00–7:00), no products were detected. Although sunlight began to illuminate the catalyst around 7:25, the CO signal remained negligible at 8:00 due to low light intensity. Measurable CO production was not observed until 9:00. The hourly CO yield reached a maximum of 9.3 μmol between 13:00 and 14:00. After 17:50, solar irradiation was no longer sufficient to maintain the reaction. Accordingly, no further increase in CO concentration was observed after the 18:00 sampling point. The variation in CO generation rate closely followed the trend of solar light intensity (Fig. 5e, g), confirming that natural sunlight can effectively trigger the CO2-to-CO reduction reaction. Although there is still plenty of room to improve overall efficiency, likely due to limitations in light collection by the simple reaction setup, our results suggest the synthesized catalyst can be trigger by nature light.

## Methods

Synthesis of the WO3 catalyst
1 g of tungsten hexachloride (WCl6) was dissolved in 60 mL of ethanol. The solution was continuously stirred at room temperature for 30 min. Subsequently, the solution was transferred to a Teflon-lined autoclave, where it underwent treatment at 180 °C for 12 h. Following this process, the suspension was subjected to centrifugation, followed by repeated washes with ethanol and deionized H2O. Finally, the obtained material was dried at 70 °C and subsequently calcined in an air atmosphere at 300 °C for 1 h, resulting in the formation of the desired WO3 catalyst.

Synthesis of Ag/WO3 catalyst
100 mg of WO3 was added to 50 mL of deionized H2O, followed by ultrasonic dispersion for 1 h to achieve a homogeneous dispersion solution; the mixture was purged with Ar for 1 h and irradiated using a 300 W xenon lamp for 1 h, during which the color changed to light blue, indicating the formation of reduced W5+. Subsequently, 3 mL of silver nitrate solution (AgNO3, 1 mg/mL) was introduced into the dispersed solution and stirred at room temperature for 1 min; after stirring, the solid catalyst was separated via centrifugation and alternately washed three times with absolute ethanol and deionized H2O. Finally, the washed catalyst was dried at 70 °C in air and calcined in an air atmosphere at 300 °C for 1 h, yielding a light-yellow product corresponding to Ag/WO3; the procedure was replicated to prepare samples with varying Ag contents by adjusting the AgNO3 addition amount accordingly.

Synthesis of composite catalyst
10 mg of cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc, analytical grade) was dissolved in 50 mL of absolute ethanol, followed by 3 h of ultrasonic treatment at room temperature. Subsequently, 90 mg of Ag/WO3 was added to the mixture, and an additional hour of ultrasonic treatment was applied. The dispersion was then ball-milled at 500 rpm for 5 h. Next, the ultrasonically treated catalyst was stirred at 85 °C until all the ethanol had evaporated. The resulting dried catalyst was washed three times with absolute ethanol and air-dried at 70 °C. The resulting catalyst is denoted as CoPc/Ag/WO3. The synthesis steps for other proportional CoPc catalysts remain the same as described above, with the only variation being the ratio of CoPc added. By substituting Ag/WO3 with WO3, while keeping the other steps unchanged, the resulting catalyst is CoPc/WO3. The detailed synthesis procedures for Cu2O and highly crystalline C3N4 are described in the Supporting Information. Upon obtaining the individual Cu2O and C3N4 monomers, the Cu2O/Ag/WO3 catalyst and the C3N4/Ag/WO3 composite catalyst were respectively prepared following a synthesis procedure analogous to that used for CoPc/Ag/WO3.

General characterization
The XRD patterns were tested using a Panalytical X’pert Pro X-ray diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.5406 Å, 40 kV, 40 mA). Raman spectra were recorded using a Raman microscope imaging spectrometer (Thermo Scientific DXR2xi, USA). XPS data were recorded using a Thermo ESCALAB 250 X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (USA). All the binding energies were referenced to the C 1s peak at 284.8 eV. To present the data intuitively, the data presented in the VB spectrum have been calibrated using the contact potential difference and the work function of the instrument36,40. EPR spectra were collected by a ELEXSYS E500 spectrometer (Bruker, Germany) at room temperature. Ag K-edge XAFS spectrum was collected at the 14W1 beamline in Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility. UV-Vis DRS spectra were carried on a Varian Cary 100 Scan UV-Vis system with BaSO4 as the reflectance standard. The transient absorption setup utilized an Yb:KGW laser in conjunction with the pump-probe transient absorption spectrometer (TA100, Time-Tech Spectra, LLC). The fundamental beam was split into two branches. One branch was directed into an optical parametric amplifier to generate the pump pulse. Meanwhile, the broadband probe pulse (ranging from 300 to 1000 nm) was produced by focusing the fundamental pulse onto a sapphire crystal. At the sample position, the focal size of pump was adjusted to be significantly larger than that of the probe, ensuring nearly homogeneous excitation density in the probed area. The samples were pumped at 360 nm and coated onto quartz glass for testing.

Evaluation of CO2 conversion performance
The photocatalytic activity of the as-prepared samples for CO2 reduction was investigated using a custom-made cylindrical stainless-steel reactor (volume = 200 mL) equipped with a quartz window. The photocatalysts (5 mg) were uniformly dispersed in 3 mL of deionized H2O and then transferred to a dish (50 mm in diameter). The dish was subsequently dried under vacuum at 70 °C for 24 h to coat it with the sample. Next, the dish with the sample was placed inside the reactor, and 1 mL of deionized H2O was added to the reactor. The reactor was purged with high-purity CO2 three times. Following this, a specific amount of high-purity CO2 was introduced into the reactor to maintain a pressure of 1 bar. Simulated sunlight was generated using a 300 W Xe arc lamp with an AM 1.5G filter, which irradiated the sample through the quartz window. The resulting products were analyzed using gas chromatography (7890B, Agilent). The instrument was equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) to detect CH4 and CO, as well as a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) to detect O2 and H2. In the isotope labeling experiment, we substituted 13CO2 for 12CO2 as the reactant, and the resulting product was detected using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (7890A and 5975C, Agilent).

Supplementary note 4. DFT calculation details
All density functional theory (DFT) computations were executed using the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP) 13. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof exchange-correlation functional (PBE-GGA) was adopted 14. Structural models were constructed based on experimental results from XRD, Raman, and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectroscopy, while possible reaction pathways were initially proposed according to insights from in situ FTIR spectroscopy. A substantial 20 Å vacuum region was implemented in surface models to prevent artificial interactions between periodic replicas. Specific computational parameters included an energy cutoff of 520 eV and a Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh of 3×3×1. For geometry optimization, convergence criteria required energy differences per atom below 10-5 eV and forces less than 0.03 eV/Å. To determine the Gibbs free energy relevant to reaction conditions, we applied the formula:
G = E_DFT + E_ZPE + E_enthalpy - T*S (1)
Here, E_DFT corresponds to the static electronic energy at absolute zero, E_ZPE to the zero-point energy correction, E_enthalpy to the enthalpy contribution, and T*S to the entropy contribution. The VESTA software package was used for visualizing all structural models 15.
